source.title: Can we avoid Double Descent in Deep Neural Networks?

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The supplied venue information conflicts with the paper text, which says it was accepted for publication at ICIP23.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps sparsity by iterative pruning, rewinding, and retraining, and measures test accuracy. This conceptually tests double descent along a parameter-count axis, but differs from a direct sweep over model architectures or sizes.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own pruning-sparsity results in Fig. 2 and a regularization ablation in Fig. 3. Epoch-wise and sample-size claims, and the broader cross-model-class claim, appear only in background discussion or citations, not as results of this study. Plotted numerical values are not legible in the provided text; rows record the outcomes described in prose.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps parameter count by iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding and retraining. It reports test accuracy and loss for LeNet on MNIST and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100 with label noise, with and without ℓ2 regularization. It also ablates the regularization strength λ. This is a different method (sparse double descent) aimed at the model-wise curve (V1) and at whether regularization removes the peak (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find ℓ2 regularization dodges double descent in the simple LeNet/MNIST setup but not in the ResNet-18/CIFAR experiments, even at high λ. They conclude an extra learning ingredient is needed, while framing the result hopefully: double descent is 'potentially avoidable'.
record.recipe_differences: Uses iterative magnitude pruning, rewinding, and retraining to vary sparsity, rather than a direct model-size sweep; compares vanilla training with ℓ2 regularization.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome differs between LeNet-300-100 on MNIST and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100. For LeNet, the reported curve changes with ℓ2 regularization; for the ResNet experiments, double descent remains with or without it. The λ ablation also reports a performance cost at extremely high regularization.
record.peer_reviewed: Accepted for publication at the International Conference on Image Processing (ICIP23), as stated in the text; supplied venue says International Conference on Information Photonics.
record.problems: Curve values are presented in figures but are not numerically legible in the supplied text. The qualitative outcome is described in prose; no uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: Only neural networks are tested; other model classes appear only in citations.

There is no noise-free control, so the study does not show that label noise drives the peak. It does not test for multiple peaks. It tunes λ over a coarse grid of four values, not to an established optimum.

missing.what: Per-ε curves showing whether the peak grows with noise level, and per-ε vanilla-vs-ℓ2 differences; only an aggregate 'on average' statement is in the prose
Train-loss curves at each λ showing the training set is no longer fit at high λ (the cost of regularization)

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study, so verdicts are allowed. All evidence is qualitative prose plus figures whose plotted values are not legible; no uncertainty is reported. The pruning-with-rewinding axis follows He et al. (sparse double descent), not width scaling. The venue in the text is ICIP23.

versions.untested_parts: Tests accuracy across pruning-induced sparsity, not a sweep over independently sized architectures.
No test-error curve over training epochs is reported.
No sweep over training sample size is reported.
No results across model classes beyond the tested neural networks; cited studies are not this study's results.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated across size, epochs, or sample count.
Tests regularization and label-noise settings in pruning experiments. Does not establish that noise drives the peak, test for multiple peaks, or test optimally tuned regularization.
Does not recalculate complexity using an effective parameter count or test whether the curve becomes an ordinary U-shape.
